accuracy.evidence: Every worked example was checked by hand: 3 packs of 4 is 12 (Sam's 4 + 3 = 7 is the planted slip), 12 sweets dealt to 3 is 4 rounds of 4, 52 − 17 = 35 by exchanging a ten (the spoken swap gives 45), hop + ing doubles to hopping after a short vowel, and a coat with an umbrella points to rain. The EEF recommendation is quoted accurately as modelling plan, monitor, evaluate.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the beliefs teachers report when introducing think-alouds: that it means saying the answer louder, that it is about speed, that a feeling ('I am rubbish at this') counts as a step, that narrating actions without reasons is enough, and that it is babyish or only for teachers. Each is named in the adult text, the sort step and the challenge feedback.

lab_distinct.evidence: A new canvas lab built for this topic: hidden thought bubbles that must be revealed one by one before the slip can be tapped, a four-slot plan, how, do, check ordering board, a talk card dragged into Helps or Doesn't help, three spoken workings with a slip to catch, and sentence starters dropped onto task moments. It passed the 30% shingle gate against every other flag lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The sequence first shows why thinking aloud matters (a bare wrong answer cannot be diagnosed until the steps are heard), then gives its structure (plan, how, do, check), then what counts as useful talk, then practises using it to catch slips in maths, spelling and reading, and ends with starters the child can use. Each success line states the idea the child has just shown.

predictions.evidence: Four locked predictions are each tested by the activity that follows: whether the answer 7 alone shows the error (then the hidden steps reveal it), whether 'Um … done!' counts as thinking aloud (then it lands in Doesn't help), why the slips can be caught (then three are caught from speech alone), and what to say when stuck (then the stuck starter is placed).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions with wrong-answer messages tagged by belief: speed, answer only, feeling not a step, only teachers, missed the slip in 6 × 5 said as 6 + 5, and checking before planning. Each message says why the choice is wrong and what useful talk sounds like instead, and the streak count resets on a miss.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences and a worked story (Sam's pens) within the learner kid FK limit; the adult text, within its limit, names metacognition, monitoring and the think-aloud protocol with plain explanations. Canvas bubbles hold one short spoken sentence each and wrap to the bubble width on a phone.

no_filler.evidence: Passed the filler phrase scan and the 12% duplication gate. Each kid paragraph has one job (what it is, why it helps, the pattern, what does not help); the adult text gives the evidence base, three reasons it works, named mistakes and what the lab does; the family tip is one modelling routine plus a listening swap.

mobile.evidence: Checked on the iPhone 13 walkthrough and 390 px screenshots of every step before and after Show me: bubbles wrap within the canvas, the order board's labels were widened so '4 Check' no longer touches its slot, the sort bins list the sorted talk legibly, and every drag has a full-width button twin.

accessibility.evidence: axe WCAG 2.1 AA was clean in light and dark themes on desktop and phone. Buttons carry full aria-labels (for example 'Sam slipped at thought 3: So I will add 4 and 3'), and the canvas aria-label repeats each spoken thought and feedback line, so the whole lab can be done with a keyboard and screen reader.
